tests.title: Work emails: examples, reactions and advice

groups.heading: Questions 1–3
groups.answerInstruction: Write NO MORE THAN ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

questions.prompt: A greeting missing from the emails Rachel dislikes: {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: Rachel objects to a name-only opening without a greeting such as hi.

questions.prompt: Reply received after a carefully written email: a single {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: The second listener received only one emoji in reply to a considered message.

questions.prompt: Number of weekly achievements requested in the government-workers example: {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: The example email requested five accomplishments from that week.

groups.heading: Questions 4–6
groups.instruction: Choose the correct answer, A, B or C.
groups.answerInstruction: Choose ONE letter for each answer.

questions.prompt: What might someone do in a fight response?

evidence.summary: Russell associates fight with domination and belittling.

distractors.B: Avoidance is described as flight, not fight.
distractors.C: Getting a task out of the way is part of the flight account.

options.label: A
options.text: Try to dominate or belittle another person.

options.label: B
options.text: Avoid opening the message.

options.label: C
options.text: Give a short reply to remove a task.

questions.prompt: Why might senior staff be copied into the hostile email example?

evidence.summary: Copying senior personnel is presented as a way to elevate an issue and diminish someone.

distractors.A: Removing the sender's name is not the example given.
distractors.B: The example is hostile escalation rather than recognition of good work.

options.label: A
options.text: To remove the sender's name from the discussion.

options.label: B
options.text: To thank the person who completed the work.

options.label: C
options.text: To raise the issue and put someone in their place.

questions.prompt: Which action is given as an example of flight?

evidence.summary: Flight can involve silence or a reply that does not address all points.

distractors.A: Escalation to senior personnel is another fight example.
distractors.C: Hostile language appears in the fight account.

options.label: A
options.text: Copying senior staff to escalate an issue.

options.label: B
options.text: Not replying or leaving points unanswered.

options.label: C
options.text: Writing in a hostile tone.

groups.heading: Questions 7–8
groups.answerInstruction: Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.

questions.prompt: The example boss gives someone else the {{blank}} for work that you did.

evidence.summary: The group-email example misattributes credit for the recipient's work.

questions.prompt: Getting a task off your plate means removing it from your own {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: The presenter explains the idiom as transferring something from one's own workload.

groups.heading: Questions 9–10
groups.answerInstruction: Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer.

questions.prompt: Besides tired, how can someone feel when doing too many things at once? {{blank}}

evidence.summary: The explanation of being frazzled includes anxiety as well as tiredness.

questions.prompt: What action is recommended before pressing send when angry? {{blank}}

evidence.summary: The recommendation is to pause before sending an angry email.

sourceReview.method: Official BBC transcript meaning cross-checked with the direct lesson recording; word-timed ASR used only to locate passages.

groups.heading: Questions 1–3
groups.instruction: Choose the correct answer, A, B or C.
groups.answerInstruction: Choose ONE letter for each answer.

questions.prompt: Why does Rachel dislike the name-only opening?

evidence.summary: Rachel links unnecessary formality with an immediate defensive reaction.

distractors.B: Her name is present; the missing element is a greeting.
distractors.C: Forwarding difficulty is not the reason she gives.

options.label: A
options.text: Its formality makes her feel defensive.

options.label: B
options.text: It suggests that the sender has forgotten her name.

options.label: C
options.text: It makes the message harder to forward.

questions.prompt: What contrast explains the second listener's complaint?

evidence.summary: The listener's effort contrasts with the minimal response of one emoji.

distractors.A: The complaint concerns a single emoji, not a lengthy formal response.
distractors.B: Escalation to senior staff appears later, not in this listener's example.

options.label: A
options.text: An informal greeting received a long formal reply.

options.label: B
options.text: An unanswered message was sent to senior staff.

options.label: C
options.text: A carefully composed message received a minimal reply.

questions.prompt: What framework is introduced to explain rude workplace messages?

evidence.summary: The psychological framework concerns responses to stress.

distractors.A: Internet access is not presented as the explanation.
distractors.C: The account concerns reactions to stress, not a message-length rule.

options.label: A
options.text: A difference between home and office internet access.

options.label: B
options.text: A stress-related fight-or-flight response.

options.label: C
options.text: A fixed rule about the number of words in an email.

groups.heading: Questions 4–6
groups.answerInstruction: Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer.

questions.prompt: Possible aim of the fight response: to {{blank}} other people.

evidence.summary: Russell names domination as one expression of a fight response.

questions.prompt: People added to an email to escalate an issue: {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: Senior personnel are copied into the message in the escalation example.

questions.prompt: A self-protective flight response may involve {{blank}} or avoiding.

evidence.summary: Russell describes withdrawal and avoidance as forms of self-protection.

evidence.summary: The boss gives another person credit for work done by the recipient.

questions.prompt: From what does a person remove a task when getting it off their plate? {{blank}}

evidence.summary: The explanation concerns removing a task from the sender's own workload.

groups.heading: Questions 9–10
groups.answerInstruction: Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.

questions.prompt: Russell describes the overloaded working environment as leaving people {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: Russell uses frazzled to characterise the state of people working in these environments.

questions.prompt: Before sending a message written in anger, the speaker recommends a {{blank}}.

tests.title: Hostility and avoidance: following the examples

groups.heading: Questions 1–3
groups.answerInstruction: Write NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS for each answer.

questions.prompt: What appears on its own at the start of the emails that annoy Rachel? {{blank}}

evidence.summary: The offending opening uses the recipient's name alone without a greeting.

questions.prompt: What was the entire response to another listener's carefully worded email? {{blank}}

evidence.summary: The listener received a single emoji rather than a substantive written response.

questions.prompt: What alternative to listing achievements was included in the employment email? {{blank}}

evidence.summary: The example required workers to list accomplishments or resign.

groups.heading: Questions 4–6
groups.answerInstruction: Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.

questions.prompt: In a fight response, an email may be {{blank}} in its tone and wording.

evidence.summary: Russell characterises fight-response emails as hostile in tone and language.

questions.prompt: A sender may copy senior {{blank}} to raise the status of a dispute.

evidence.summary: The escalation example involves copying senior personnel.

questions.prompt: People may protect themselves in a flight response by {{blank}} from the exchange.

evidence.summary: Withdrawal is explicitly described as a protective flight response.

groups.heading: Questions 7–8
groups.instruction: Choose the correct answer, A, B or C.
groups.answerInstruction: Choose ONE letter for each answer.

questions.prompt: What is the effect intended by the boss who credits someone else for your work?

evidence.summary: The example illustrates putting a worker in their place by withholding deserved credit.

distractors.A: No changed deadline is part of the boss's group email.
distractors.C: The example takes away recognition; it does not complete the person's tasks.

options.label: A
options.text: To explain why a deadline has changed.

options.label: B
options.text: To lower your sense of importance.

options.label: C
options.text: To reduce your workload by completing the work.

questions.prompt: What do the silence and quick, unhelpful reply have in common?

evidence.summary: Both behaviours illustrate moving work away from oneself rather than resolving it.

distractors.B: Senior managers are part of the earlier escalation example.
distractors.C: Misassigned credit is the separate boss example.

options.label: A
options.text: Both can help the sender avoid dealing with a task.

options.label: B
options.text: Both explicitly involve senior managers.

options.label: C
options.text: Both give another worker public credit.

tests.title: Workplace tone: recognising intentions and causal links

groups.heading: Questions 1–3
groups.answerInstruction: Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.

questions.prompt: Rachel interprets unnecessary formality as putting her on the {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: Rachel describes an immediate defensive reaction to the overly formal opening.

questions.prompt: The second complaint centres on a single {{blank}} replacing a substantive response.

evidence.summary: A minimal emoji response is contrasted with the effort put into the original message.

questions.prompt: The employment email asked workers to list what they had {{blank}} that week.

evidence.summary: The request concerned things the workers had accomplished during that week.

groups.heading: Questions 4–6
groups.instruction: Choose the correct answer, A, B or C.
groups.answerInstruction: Choose ONE letter for each answer.

questions.prompt: What purpose makes the fight response more than a simple failure to answer?

evidence.summary: The fight response involves active domination or belittling rather than withdrawal.

distractors.A: Reducing one's workload through incomplete engagement belongs to flight.
distractors.C: Avoidance and silence are described as flight responses.

options.label: A
options.text: An attempt to remove tasks without addressing all their details.

options.label: B
options.text: An attempt to assert dominance or reduce another person's standing.

options.label: C
options.text: An attempt to avoid the issue by leaving it unanswered.

questions.prompt: In Russell's particular example, why is copying management hostile?

evidence.summary: The hostile meaning comes from the stated purpose of the copying, not merely the use of email.

distractors.B: Work avoidance is the flight example, not the purpose of this escalation.
distractors.C: Recognition is the opposite of putting someone in their place here.

options.label: A
options.text: It is used to escalate the dispute and diminish the recipient.

options.label: B
options.text: It is used to pass the sender's tasks away without discussing them.

options.label: C
options.text: It is used to acknowledge the recipient's completed work.

questions.prompt: What explains the incomplete reply in the flight account?

evidence.summary: Failure to address all points serves a withdrawal strategy that removes the matter from the sender's plate.

distractors.A: Escalation and authority are part of the fight account.
distractors.B: Public recognition is not the motive assigned to the incomplete reply.

options.label: A
options.text: The sender is escalating the matter to establish authority.

options.label: B
options.text: The sender is trying to provide public recognition for a colleague.

options.label: C
options.text: The sender is seeking protection through avoidance, not full resolution.

groups.heading: Questions 7–8
groups.answerInstruction: Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.

questions.prompt: What an avoidant sender wants to reduce: their own {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: The explanation identifies the sender's workload as what is being reduced through transfer.

questions.prompt: Time pressure cited as an obstacle to consistently polite writing: a {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: The speaker identifies deadline pressure alongside stress.

groups.heading: Questions 9–10
groups.answerInstruction: Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer.

questions.prompt: Which emotional state accompanies tiredness in the explanation of overload? {{blank}}

evidence.summary: Anxiety is paired with tiredness in the explanation of feeling frazzled.

questions.prompt: What interruption to the sending process does the advice recommend? {{blank}}

evidence.summary: The recommended safeguard is a pause before sending an angry message.

tests.title: Email behaviour: separating avoidance from confrontation

groups.heading: Questions 1–3
groups.answerInstruction: Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.

questions.prompt: Feature Rachel finds needlessly distancing: {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: Rachel specifically identifies unnecessary formality as the source of discomfort.

questions.prompt: Minimal reply contrasted with a carefully composed message: a single {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: The mismatch in the second listener's account is between considered writing and one emoji.

questions.prompt: State associated with the psychological response discussed: being {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: The explanatory framework concerns how people react when stressed.

groups.heading: Questions 4–6
groups.instruction: Choose the correct answer, A, B or C.
groups.answerInstruction: Choose ONE letter for each answer.

questions.prompt: Which behaviour belongs to confrontation rather than withdrawal in Russell's account?

evidence.summary: The contrast places domination in fight and disengagement in flight.

distractors.B: An unanswered email is used as an example of avoiding engagement.
distractors.C: A reply that omits points is another form of avoidance.

options.label: A
options.text: Trying to dominate the other person.

options.label: B
options.text: Leaving the email unanswered.

options.label: C
options.text: Answering only selected points.

questions.prompt: What is the intended function of adding senior personnel in the example?

evidence.summary: The copied managers are used to elevate the issue and assert a status difference.

distractors.A: Task avoidance is the following flight explanation, not the stated purpose of the copying.
distractors.B: The opening-greeting complaint is separate from the deliberate escalation example.

options.label: A
options.text: To give the sender time to reduce the number of tasks on their plate.

options.label: B
options.text: To correct a neutral greeting that sounded too formal.

options.label: C
options.text: To increase the stakes of the issue and put the recipient in their place.

questions.prompt: What common purpose links withdrawal and avoidance in the flight response?

evidence.summary: Russell describes withdrawal and avoidance as ways people protect themselves.

distractors.A: Informing management is not the purpose stated for withdrawing.
distractors.C: Belittling another person is attached to fight, not flight.

options.label: A
options.text: Giving a manager better information.

options.label: B
options.text: Self-protection.

options.label: C
options.text: Publicly diminishing another worker.

groups.heading: Questions 7–8
groups.answerInstruction: Write NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS for each answer.

questions.prompt: What does the boss allocate to another person in the status-lowering example? {{blank}}

evidence.summary: The boss attributes the recipient's work to someone else through a group email.

questions.prompt: What does an avoidant colleague try to take the task out of? {{blank}}

evidence.summary: The idiom is explained as moving tasks out of one's own workload.

groups.heading: Questions 9–10
groups.answerInstruction: Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.

questions.prompt: Russell uses {{blank}} to describe the overloaded state associated with greater incivility.

evidence.summary: The state of being frazzled is linked to increased risk, not certainty, of incivility.

questions.prompt: A sender who is angry is advised to {{blank}} rather than dispatch the message immediately.

evidence.summary: The advice introduces a pause before the send action.
